claims.claim: what part of this code scares you?
Organise by feature type, each entry phrased as a testable attack
no trimming | enter " value " with spaces
length not checked server-side | 10,000-char string via API
rounding | 0.005 amounts, currency with 0 or 3 decimals
timezone | create at 23:30 local in UTC+10
empty / one / pagination edge | 0, 1, page-size, page-size+1 items
double submit | double-click Pay, browser back after submit
unhandled dependency failure | stub returns 500 / timeout
odd names | unicode, spaces, 255 chars, same name twice
IDOR | change ID in URL to another user's
claims.note: IDOR appears on neither page; the glossary root URL returns an empty JavaScript application shell (1827 bytes, no term definitions) to non-browser fetchers, so no glossary definitions could be read.

claims.claim: turn entries into a short charter or checklist
Log which entries found defects; promote them, retire entries that never find anything.
Feed recurring faults into prevention: lint rules, shared validators, review checklist.
A generic list gets stale and ignored; keep it product-specific and short per section.
Error guessing finds only what someone imagined; combine with systematic techniques.
The fault list is versioned, each entry has a source (defect ID or taxonomy), and session notes reference which entries were applied.

coverage: Every concrete claim in the skill was checked: the CTFL v4.0 4.4.1 citation, all named external references (Kaner/Falk/Nguyen, Beizer, OWASP Top 10, ODC, IDOR), every number (6-12 months, 10,000-char, 0.005, 0 and 3 decimals, 23:30, UTC+10, 0, 1, page-size+1, 500, 255 chars) and every behaviour in the fault table, process steps and gotchas; the skill has no commands or flags.
